w: Cast in wrought iron in 1389, the movement inside this Renaissance arch is roughly twice the size of the Wells Cathedral clock and among the oldest of its kind still running in France. The golden sun-face dial shows the phases of the moon and the day of the week, and after a 1997 restoration it still keeps time.
s: One of the oldest working clock movements in France
_facts: Astronomical clock from the 14th century, movement made in 1389, among the oldest such mechanisms in France
Roughly twice the size of the Wells Cathedral clock movement
Renaissance facade added 1529; electrified 1920s, restored 1997; dial shows moon phases and days of the week

w: A 13th-century shrine to the Virgin Mary once stood here before it was rebuilt and enlarged in 1840 into France's first church built in the Gothic Revival style. Nearly every window, sculpture and carved detail seems to carry some donor's name or coat of arms - a basilica built almost entirely on gratitude.
s: France's first Gothic Revival church, on a 1200s shrine
_facts: First church in France built in the Gothic Revival style
Original shrine dedicated to the Virgin Mary dates to the 13th century, reconstructed and enlarged in 1840
Highly ornate decoration with windows and sculptures often bearing a donor's name or coat of arms

w: Opened in 2008 after four years of construction, this vertical-lift bridge raises its road deck like an elevator to let tall ships pass beneath on the Seine. Rouen's city council named it for Gustave Flaubert, the novelist born and buried here - a rare bridge honouring a writer instead of a general.
s: A bridge that lifts its deck for ships, named for a novelist
_facts: Vertical-lift bridge over the Seine, opened 25 September 2008 after construction begun 2004
Named after novelist Gustave Flaubert, who was born and died in Rouen

n: Church of St Joan of Arc
w: Completed in 1979 on the Place du Vieux-Marche, this modern church marks the exact spot where Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for heresy in 1431 - a small garden called Le Bucher, 'the pyre', sits just outside it. Its sweeping curves are meant to evoke both flames and an overturned longship.
s: A church shaped like flames, built where Joan of Arc burned
_facts: Catholic church completed 1979 on the Place du Vieux-Marche, where Joan of Arc was burned at the stake in 1431
Le Bucher ('the pyre') garden outside marks the exact execution spot
Designed by architect Louis Arretche; sweeping curves evoke flames and an overturned longship

w: This fortified ducal and royal residence, seat of the duchy of Normandy, was torn down at the end of the 16th century, its stone hauled off for other buildings around Rouen. Only one tower survived, restored by Viollet-le-Duc in the 19th century and long linked to Joan of Arc - a link historians now doubt.
s: The 'Joan of Arc tower' that was never actually hers
_facts: Chateau Bouvreuil, fortified ducal and royal residence in Rouen, capital of the duchy of Normandy
Destroyed at the end of the 16th century, stone reused for other construction
Surviving tower wrongly associated with Joan of Arc, restored by Viollet-le-Duc in the 19th century

w: A Scottish banker named John Law once owned this walled garden before Napoleon bought it in 1811 to house a Seine prefecture. In between, two women launched themselves from it by air: Sophie Blanchard by balloon in 1806, Elisa Garnerin by parachute in 1817. Today it holds over 5,600 plant taxa, fuchsias included.
s: A balloonist's launch pad turned 5,600-species garden
_facts: 8-hectare municipal botanical garden, dates to a walled garden built by Louis de Carel in 1691, later owned by Scottish banker John Law
Sophie Blanchard made a solo balloon ascension from the grounds in 1806; Elisa Garnerin parachuted from a balloon here in 1817
Napoleon purchased the garden in 1811; opened to the public 1817 and today holds over 5,600 plant taxa, notable fuchsia collection

w: Built between 1499 and 1507 to house the Exchequer of Normandy, this building became the seat of the Parliament of Normandy under Francois I, then a courthouse after the Revolution. A bombing raid on 26 August 1944 nearly destroyed its Louis XII-style core; restoration wasn't finished until 1979.
s: A Renaissance parliament house rebuilt from WWII rubble
_facts: Former Echiquier de Normandie, built 1499-1507; became seat of the Parliament of Normandy under Francois I in 1515
Functioned as courthouse from the French Revolution onward
Bombed 26 August 1944, nearly destroying the Louis XII-style main building; classified historical monument 1840, restoration inscribed complete 1977/1979

w: Set up in 1831 to house finds excavated at Lillebonne, this museum survived a fire in 1894 and now holds the archaeological record of Seine-Maritime under one roof. Early curator Jean Benoit Desire Cochet helped shape French archaeology itself; the collection has outlived him by well over a century.
s: Norman archaeology, rescued from a dig - then a fire
_facts: Museum of France, set up 1831 to house finds from excavations at Lillebonne
Suffered a fire on 21 April 1894
Early curator was archaeologist Jean Benoit Desire Cochet; joined the Reunion des Musees Metropolitains Rouen Normandie network in 2016

w: Guillaume Le Roux built this stone townhouse at the end of the 15th century to match his rank on the Exchequer of Normandy, and his son finished the job. Its courtyard gallery carries a sculpted scene of the Field of the Cloth of Gold, the meeting of Francis I and Henry VIII - now backdrop to a five-star hotel.
s: A Renaissance townhouse carved with a meeting of kings
_facts: Former hotel particulier at 15 place de la Pucelle, mostly 16th century, monument historique since 1924
Aumale Gallery shows Renaissance sculpture of the Field of the Cloth of Gold meeting between Francis I and Henry VIII
Damaged in WWII bombing, later a bank, now a deluxe hotel reopened in 2010

w: Opened in 1828 to the northeast of the old town, this is Rouen's most important cemetery - its gate, chapel and monumental cross all designed by the same hand, Charles Felix Maillet du Boullay. Wander its slopes and you're walking through two centuries of the city's dead, laid out with real architectural ambition.
s: Rouen's grandest cemetery, gated by its own architect
_facts: Most important cemetery in Rouen, opened 1828, situated northeast of the town centre
Entrance gate, chapel and monumental cross designed by Charles Felix Maillet du Boullay

w: Formally the Theatre des Arts, this opera house anchors a small network of venues across the city, including the deconsecrated Chapelle Corneille down the road. It houses the Rouen Philharmonic Orchestra and sits close enough to the Metro and TEOR lines that you can hear the trams between movements.
s: Home to the Rouen Philharmonic, steps from the tram
_facts: Formally Opera de Rouen Normandie - Theatre des arts
Home of the Rouen Philharmonic Orchestra; operates a portfolio of venues including the Chapelle Corneille
Located next to the Metro and TEOR station Theatre des arts

w: Founded in 1345, La Couronne claims the title of oldest inn in France, though no contemporary document actually backs that up. What's certain is 1948, when a young Julia Child ate her first French meal here and walked out determined to spend her life cooking. The dining room still shows off its old portraits.
s: France's oldest inn - and the meal that made Julia Child
_facts: Restaurant founded 1345, claims to be the oldest inn in France (unverified by contemporary documents)
In 1948 chef and author Julia Child ate her first French meal here, said to have inspired her culinary career
Dining room on the 1st floor displays paintings of notable figures

w: Erected in bronze in 1865 outside Rouen's city hall, this equestrian statue of Napoleon nearly got melted down by Republicans in 1881 for lack of funds. When it came down for repairs in 2020 over a cracked hoof, workers found gold, silver and bronze coins of Napoleon III sealed inside the pedestal.
s: A statue with a treasure chest hidden in its own pedestal
_facts: Equestrian statue of Napoleon at Place du General-de-Gaulle, erected 1865, sculpted by Gabriel-Vital Dubray
1881 plans to melt it down or remove the rider were dropped for lack of funds
Taken down for repairs June 2020; a treasure chest of Napoleon III-era coins found inside the pedestal

w: Built on a scale to rival Rouen Cathedral itself, this former Benedictine abbey church takes its name from Audoin, the city's 7th-century bishop. Composer Charles-Marie Widor once called its unaltered Cavaille-Coll organ 'a Michelangelo of an organ' - one of three great Gothic monuments that define Rouen's skyline.
s: A Gothic giant with an organ Widor called 'Michelangelo'
_facts: Large Gothic Catholic church, former Benedictine monastic church, named for 7th-century bishop Audoin (Ouen)
Built on a similar scale to Rouen Cathedral
Famous for its large, unaltered Cavaille-Coll organ, described by Charles-Marie Widor as 'a Michelangelo of an organ'
